lead: This unit follows one idea: a magnetic field is created and changed, and every electrical machine is built to exploit that change. After it you can compute MMF, flux and reluctance, apply Faraday's law, read a transformer's EMF equation, and explain how a DC machine, an induction motor, a synchronous machine and a BLDC motor start, what torque they produce and where each is used.
about: The unit follows one thread: a magnetic field is made and changed, and machines exploit that change. Chapter 3.1 treats the iron path as a circuit, with MMF driving flux through reluctance. Chapter 3.2 adds Faraday's law, so changing flux becomes an EMF, and defines self and mutual inductance. Chapter 3.3 applies both to the transformer, the only machine with no moving parts. Chapter 3.4 puts the same windings on a rotating armature with a commutator, giving DC generators and motors. Chapter 3.5 replaces the commutator with a three-phase rotating field in the induction motor. Chapter 3.6 explains why a single-phase field cannot start alone, and covers the universal motor. Chapter 3.7 covers synchronous machines, locked to supply frequency. Chapter 3.8 collects stepper, servo and BLDC motors, where electronics replaces brushes.

chapters.idea: A magnetic path behaves like a resistive circuit: magnetomotive force drives flux through reluctance, and an air gap dominates the total reluctance.
chapters.depth: Define flux Φ (weber), flux density B = Φ/A (tesla), magnetomotive force MMF = N·I (ampere-turns), reluctance S = l/(μ₀μᵣA) in ampere-turns per weber, and permeability μ = μ₀μᵣ with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. Build the analogy table: EMF ↔ MMF, current ↔ flux, resistance ↔ reluctance, so Φ = MMF/S replaces I = V/R. Solve one series magnetic circuit with an iron part and one air gap; show that the gap, though millimetres long, can hold most of the reluctance. Mention parallel paths (a core with a central limb) only as S in parallel, and leak-free flux as the assumption. Some syllabi call reluctance magnetic resistance and MMF magnetising force.

figure.title: Series magnetic circuit
figure.aria: A coil produces MMF, which pushes flux through the iron reluctance and then the much larger air-gap reluctance to give 0.161 mWb of flux.

chapters.example: An iron ring of mean length 50 cm and cross-section 4 cm² has a 1 mm air gap cut in it. The relative permeability of the iron is 2000 and the coil has 400 turns carrying 1 A. Find the reluctance of the iron, the reluctance of the air gap, the flux and the flux density. Take μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. Answer: iron S = 0.5/(2.513 × 10⁻³ × 4 × 10⁻⁴) = 4.97 × 10⁵ A·t/Wb; gap S = 1 × 10⁻³/(1.257 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.99 × 10⁶ A·t/Wb; total 2.49 × 10⁶; Φ = 400/2.49 × 10⁶ = 0.161 mWb; B = 0.161 × 10⁻³/4 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.40 T.
chapters.trap: Using μᵣ for the air gap, or leaving length in cm and area in cm², which shifts the answer by powers of ten; the gap needs μᵣ = 1 and metres.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for Ohm's law and series resistance, which give the analogy.
chapters.leave: Saturation, the B-H curve, hysteresis and eddy-current loss go to later courses; inductor energy is covered in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A changing flux linkage produces an EMF, and inductance is simply flux linkage per ampere, shared between coils when they share flux.
chapters.depth: State Faraday's first law (flux change makes an EMF) and second law (e = N·ΔΦ/Δt), then Lenz's law for the minus sign. Define self-inductance L = NΦ/I in henries and the induced EMF e = −L·di/dt. Define mutual inductance M = N₂Φ₂₁/I₁, coefficient of coupling k = M/√(L₁L₂), 0 ≤ k ≤ 1, and mutual EMF e₂ = M·di₁/dt. Cover inductances in series (L₁ + L₂ ± 2M) and the dot convention as a one-line rule for adding or subtracting M; only a few syllabi teach the full dot-rule algebra. Show that in a sinusoid the EMF leads the flux by 90°.

figure.aria: One 50 Hz cycle: the sinusoidal flux peaks at 5 ms and 15 ms, while the induced EMF peaks 90 degrees earlier at 0 ms and 10 ms.

chapters.example: A coil of 500 turns has its flux changed uniformly from 2 mWb to 6 mWb in 8 ms. Find the induced EMF. Two coils on one core have L₁ = 0.4 H, L₂ = 0.1 H and k = 0.6; find M and the EMF in coil 2 when the current in coil 1 rises at 50 A/s. Answer: e = 500 × (6 − 2) × 10⁻³/8 × 10⁻³ = 250 V; M = 0.6 × √(0.4 × 0.1) = 0.12 H; e₂ = 0.12 × 50 = 6 V.
chapters.trap: Dropping N, or using ΔΦ/Δt without converting mWb to Wb and ms to s; then reporting an answer a thousand times off.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for flux and flux density; Unit 2 for the phasor idea behind the 90° shift.
chapters.leave: Dot-convention circuit problems and coupled-coil transients belong to a circuits course; R-L transients are in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Two windings on one iron core share the same alternating flux, so the volts per turn are equal and voltage ratio equals turns ratio.
chapters.depth: Construction: core type and shell type, laminated silicon-steel core to cut eddy currents, windings on the limbs. Working: primary current makes an alternating flux, the flux links both windings, and each produces a counter EMF. Derive E = 4.44 f N Φm (4.44 = 4 × 1.11, the form factor of a sine wave) and show E₁/E₂ = N₁/N₂ = I₂/I₁ for an ideal transformer. Define rated kVA, turns ratio and the idea of a step-up or step-down unit. Keep losses qualitative: copper loss I²R, iron loss from hysteresis and eddy currents. Applications: transmission, phone chargers, welding sets.

figure.title: Energy transfer through the core
figure.aria: The 230 V supply drives the 460-turn primary, the core carries 2.25 mWb peak flux, and the 46-turn secondary delivers 23 V to the load.

chapters.example: A single-phase transformer is rated 230 V/23 V, 50 Hz and its primary has 460 turns. Find the secondary turns and the peak core flux. If the secondary supplies 2 A to a load, find the ideal primary current. Answer: N₂ = 460 × 23/230 = 46 turns; Φm = 230/(4.44 × 50 × 460) = 2.25 mWb; I₁ = 2 × 23/230 = 0.2 A.
chapters.trap: Putting the RMS voltage into E = 4.44 f N Φm and calling Φm an RMS flux, or writing 4 instead of 4.44 in the equation.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2; Unit 2 for RMS value and form factor.
chapters.leave: Equivalent circuit, regulation, efficiency and phasor diagrams go to a machines or power course.

chapters.idea: One machine works both ways: as a generator, rotation with flux makes a DC EMF; as a motor, DC in the armature makes torque, limited by the back EMF it produces.
chapters.depth: Construction: yoke, poles with field windings, armature with commutator and brushes. Generating action from Faraday's law; commutator plus brush converts coil AC into DC at the terminals. EMF equation E = PΦNZ/(60A) with P poles, Φ flux per pole, N speed in rpm, Z armature conductors, A parallel paths (A = P for lap, A = 2 for wave). Motor action: back EMF E_b = V − I_aR_a and torque T = PΦI_aZ/(2πA) proportional to Φ and I_a. Types by excitation: separately excited, shunt, series, compound, with one line on each speed behaviour. Applications: shunt generator for battery charging, series motor for traction and cranes.

figure.title: Motor: back EMF sets the current
figure.aria: A 230 V supply drives the field and armature, the rotating armature generates 220 V back EMF, and the remaining 10 V drives 20 A to produce shaft torque against the load.

chapters.example: A 4-pole lap-wound DC generator has 400 armature conductors, flux 0.03 Wb per pole and runs at 1500 rpm. Find the generated EMF. The same machine runs as a motor from 230 V, draws 20 A, and its armature resistance is 0.5 Ω; find the back EMF. Answer: lap means A = P = 4, so E = 0.03 × 1500 × 400/60 = 300 V; E_b = 230 − 20 × 0.5 = 220 V.
chapters.trap: Using A = 2 for a lap winding, or forgetting that A equals the number of poles only in lap winding.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2; Unit 1 for KVL around the armature circuit.
chapters.leave: Armature reaction, commutation, losses and speed-control methods go to a dedicated machines course.

chapters.idea: A three-phase winding makes a rotating field at synchronous speed; the rotor follows it with a small slip, and torque peaks at the pull-out slip before falling away.
chapters.depth: Construction: squirrel cage and slip-ring rotors, stator with three-phase winding. Rotating field: three phases 120° apart give a field of constant magnitude turning at N_s = 120f/P rpm. Define slip s = (N_s − N)/N_s and rotor frequency f_r = s·f. Torque-slip curve: near s = 0 torque is proportional to slip (stable region), maximum at pull-out slip s_m, then falls; starting torque at s = 1, full-load slip typically 2% to 5%. Relation T = air-gap power/ω_s. Applications: pumps, fans, lathe, compressors, the workhorse of industry.

figure.aria: Torque rises almost linearly up to the peak of 1 per unit at 20 percent slip and then falls to about 0.38 per unit at standstill, 100 percent slip.

chapters.example: A 4-pole, 50 Hz, three-phase induction motor runs at 4% slip. Find the synchronous speed, the rotor speed and the rotor frequency. If the air-gap power is 12 kW, find the torque. Answer: N_s = 120 × 50/4 = 1500 rpm; N = 1500(1 − 0.04) = 1440 rpm; f_r = 0.04 × 50 = 2 Hz; ω_s = 2π × 1500/60 = 157.1 rad/s, so T = 12000/157.1 = 76.4 N·m.
chapters.trap: Writing s = 4 instead of 0.04, or calling 1440 rpm the synchronous speed; the field always turns at 1500 rpm.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 for induced EMF; Unit 2 for three-phase supply and the rotating field.
chapters.leave: Equivalent circuit, circle diagram, and star-delta and autotransformer starting go to later units and courses.

chapters.idea: A single-phase winding gives a pulsating field, which can be split into forward and backward fields, so the motor needs a starting aid; the universal motor uses a commutator to run on AC or DC.
chapters.depth: Double-revolving-field picture: one pulsating field equals two equal fields turning opposite ways, so at standstill torque is zero and the motor cannot start alone. Starting methods: resistance split-phase, capacitor-start, capacitor-start capacitor-run, shaded pole; each in two lines with a typical application (fans, refrigerators, compressors). Once running, the forward field dominates and the motor produces torque. Universal motor: series DC motor with laminated field and compensating winding so it runs on AC; high speed, small size, used in mixers, drills, vacuum cleaners. Some syllabi call these fractional-kilowatt or domestic motors.

figure.title: Capacitor-start motor
figure.aria: The supply feeds the main winding and the capacitor-fed auxiliary winding; their currents nearly 90 degrees apart produce a rotating field that starts the rotor.

chapters.example: A 230 V, 50 Hz capacitor-start motor has a main winding whose current lags the supply by 70°. The auxiliary winding on its own would lag by 20°, but with a 40 μF capacitor in series its current leads by 15°. Find the phase difference between the two winding currents and say whether the motor will start. Answer: 70° + 15° = 85°, close to the 90° needed, so a rotating field appears and the motor starts. Without the capacitor the split would be only 70° − 20° = 50°, too small to start reliably.
chapters.trap: Saying a single-phase induction motor is self-starting, or that the auxiliary winding stays in circuit in all designs; in most it is cut out by a centrifugal switch.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.5 for the rotating field; Unit 2 for phase difference and impedance angle.
chapters.leave: Capacitor sizing, torque-speed curves of each split-phase type, and speed control of the universal motor go to a machines course.

chapters.idea: The rotor turns at exactly synchronous speed, locked to the supply frequency, so a synchronous machine gives fixed-speed generation and power-factor control but cannot start on its own.
chapters.depth: Construction: rotating field on the rotor, three-phase armature on the stator (cylindrical and salient-pole rotors). Generator: frequency relation f = PN/120, EMF per phase E = 4.44 f Φ T (T turns per phase in series), star line voltage √3 times phase voltage. Motor: runs only at N_s, needs a starting method such as a damper winding or a pony motor; excitation sets the power factor, giving the V-curve of armature current against field current, with unity power factor at the dip. Applications: alternators in power stations, synchronous condensers for power-factor correction, constant-speed drives.

figure.aria: The V-curve: armature current falls to a minimum of 1 per unit at 4 per unit field current, where the motor runs at unity power factor, and rises on either side.

chapters.example: A three-phase, star-connected alternator has 4 poles, runs at 1500 rpm, and each phase has 200 turns in series with a flux of 0.02 Wb per pole. Find the frequency, the EMF per phase and the line voltage. Answer: f = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz; E_ph = 4.44 × 50 × 0.02 × 200 = 888 V; line voltage = √3 × 888 = 1538 V.
chapters.trap: Thinking a synchronous motor can start by itself from the supply, or using the line voltage in a per-phase EMF equation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 for the EMF equation form; Chapter 3.5 for synchronous speed; Unit 2 for star connections.
chapters.leave: Phasor diagrams of salient-pole machines, parallel operation and hunting go to a power-systems course.

chapters.idea: Special machines trade simplicity for control: the stepper moves in fixed steps open-loop, the servo closes a loop around position, and the BLDC swaps brushes for electronic switching.
chapters.depth: Stepper: step angle β = 360°/(m·N_r) for m phases and N_r rotor teeth, steps per revolution = 360°/β, speed from pulse rate, holding torque; open-loop position control in printers and 3D printers. Servo: DC or AC motor with position or speed sensor and a controller that corrects the error; used in robot arms and CNC. BLDC: permanent-magnet rotor, stator switched by an inverter in sequence from rotor position; high efficiency and long life, used in ceiling fans, e-rickshaws and drones. Mention PMSM in one line as the sinusoidally driven cousin of the BLDC. Only a few syllabi teach stepper driver circuits.

figure.aria: Special machines split into stepper with 1.8 degrees per step in open loop, servo with feedback, and BLDC with electronic commutation, each with two typical applications.

chapters.example: A stepper motor has 4 phases and a rotor with 50 teeth. Find the step angle and the number of steps per revolution. How many pulses move the shaft through 90°, and what is the speed at 300 pulses per second? Answer: β = 360/(4 × 50) = 1.8°; steps per revolution = 200; 90° needs 50 pulses; speed = 1.8 × 300 = 540°/s = 90 rpm.
chapters.trap: Confusing step angle with steps per revolution, or claiming a stepper holds position without power; holding torque needs current in the windings.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 for the commutator and torque, Chapter 3.6 for the universal motor, Chapter 3.7 for closed-loop control.
chapters.leave: Inverter switching, PWM and driver ICs go to Units 4 and 5; magnetic design of motors goes to a machines course.
